newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Basic facts about elections in Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Basic facts about elections in Chechnya.

text.p: Voters in Chechnya, which fought a bitter war to break away from Russia, go to the polls on Monday to elect a president and a local parliament.

No foreign state has recognised Chechnya's 1991 declaration of independence and formally it remains one of the 21 ethnic-based republics which, together with 68 Russian regions, make up the Russian Federation.
Sixteen candidates are vying for a five-year presidential term.

The leading contenders are Aslan Maskhadov, the chief commander of the Chechen guerrilla army which fought off Russian troops after a 21-month war, former rebel field commander Shamil Basayev, wartime propaganda chief Movladi Udugov, and acting president Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev.
To win in the first round, candidates need to win more than half the votes cast (50 percent plus one vote).
If no candidate achieves this, a runoff round will be held two weeks later between the two candidates with most votes.
If fewer than 50 percent of voters registered on electoral rolls take part in either the first or second rounds, then that round is declared invalid and is repeated within one month.
The Central Election Commission says about 850 candidates are seeking election to the 63-member parliament, which will also serve for five years.
All seats are allocated on the basis of single-member constituencies, although candidates may list party affiliation.

Under the constitution the president appoints ministers, who must be approved by a majority in parliament. But he or she has power to disband the body, as the late president Dzhokhar Dudayev did in 1993.
Voters may cast ballots in 423 regular polling places from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. (0400 to 1700 GMT) on Monday.
Preliminary results are expected to start coming in on Tuesday and final results must be certified and published within five days of the end of voting.

The Central Election Commission puts the registered electorate at approximately 400,000, but the figure does not include refugees who will vote in special stations or persons who returned to the republic recently.

The Commission says it will open more than a dozen special polling places near Chechnya's borders with the neighbouring Russian republics of Ingushetia and Dagestan, as well as the Stavropol region, where most refugees from the conflict are believed to be concentrated.
Transport arrangements are being made to bring refugees in these areas to vote. The Central Election Commission says it expects between 50,000 and 60,000 refugees to cast ballots in these stations.
Chechnya's prewar population has been estimated at around one million but tens of thousands of people were killed in the 1994-96 conflict and thousands more fled fighting.
Most of the minority ethnic Russian population is believed to have left the historically Moslem republic.

The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) has been assisting Chechnya in organising voting and has allocated more than $500,000 for funding the printing of ballots, the construction of ballot boxes and the purchase of indelible ink skin-marking devices to prevent double voting.
The OSCE says more than 60 observers will monitor voting under its auspices.
